2422087:
Welcome to the Unstucking Pathway!

This is your first step of many. Each one gets you closer to getting unstuck and living a life with more calm, confidence, and connection.

You’re on the Pathway, but you’re not alone. I’ll walk with you every single step, but there are also other Unstucking Academy students.

Let’s make it official.

Take this next small step:
2422088:
Your journey follows a clear, three-stage roadmap. This structure guides you step-by-step, ensuring you have the right tools at the right time.

Stage 1: Understanding the Foundation: The starting point for everyone. Dive into Polyvagal Theory in a simple way to reduce shame and blame, and build a more compassionate lens for yourself. (Even if you think you know it, don't skip this!

Stage 2: Building Your Safety: Actively strengthen your connection to safety with practices that build more calm, confidence, and motivation in your daily life. This stage can take time, and that's perfectly okay.

Stage 3: Compassionately Unstucking: Learn to mindfully feel your defensive states while anchored in the safety you built in Stage 2, allowing for natural self-regulation. The key here is: don't rush it.

A Quick Note on Videos:These videos come from programs I've created over the years. If you hear an old program name, you can just ignore it and focus on the content.
2422094:
Let's start with the biology that powers your entire experience. The Autonomic Nervous System (ANS) is the foundation of everything we'll explore in Polyvagal Theory.

Your Body's Autopilot: Are you consciously planning your breathing or heart rate right now? Probably not. The ANS is the unconscious system that handles all of this for you, freeing up your mind to focus on other things. This automatic regulation is a key survival feature.

Beyond Fight or Flight: The old "fight or flight" vs. "rest and digest" model is incomplete. Polyvagal Theory reveals a more nuanced picture with three distinct neural circuits, or "platforms," that regulate your body's activity: safety, flight/fight, and shutdown.

How Biology Shapes Your World: These three platforms are the foundation for your physiological state. Depending on which one is active, they directly influence your feelings, thoughts, and behaviors, shifting you between states of safety and defense.
2422105:
Let's visualize how your nervous system works using a metaphor: The Polyvagal Ladder. This is a simple way to understand the hierarchy of your autonomic states.

The Three Rungs of Experience: Your nervous system has three main states, organized like a ladder. At the top is your Safe & Social state (connection), in the middle is Flight/Fight (mobilization), and at the bottom is Shutdown (immobilization).

A Sequence, Not a Menu: This isn't a menu of options you choose from. Your body moves up or down the ladder one rung at a time. These are unconscious, biological responses, not conscious decisions.

It's All About Survival:As you move down the ladder, you lose access to the abilities of the higher rungs (like social connection when you're in fight/flight). This isn't a weakness; it's your biology's way of prioritizing what's needed for survival in that moment.
2424265:
Your Polyvagal state is the filter through which you experience reality. It's not just a mood; it's the biological context for everything you think, feel, and do.

A Reaction to Your World (Inside & Out): Your state constantly shifts based on your external environment (like the room you're in), your internal sensations (like hunger or pain), and your unique perceptions shaped by past experiences.

The Lens That Colors Everything: Whether you're in a safe, flight/fight, or shutdown state directly impacts how you experience the world. The same situation can feel completely different depending on the state you're in.
2422106:
Ever get a "gut feeling" or a "spidey sense" about a person or place? That's your neuroception at work. It's your body's built-in, unconscious system for detecting cues of safety and danger.

Your Body's Surveillance System: Your body is constantly evaluating your internal and external world for cues of safety or risk. This happens automatically, through your five senses, without you even having to think about it.

An Unconscious Process: Neuroception is not a conscious choice. Information from your senses is sent to your brainstem, which then triggers a biological response to keep you safe. You are hardwired for this.

Shifting Your State: This unconscious evaluation is what moves you up or down your Polyvagal Ladder. It's a survival mechanism that activates your social or defensive states based on the cues it detects.
2426599:
Is your body's "danger detector" properly calibrated? Sometimes, our internal alarm system gets its wires crossed. This lesson explores the difference between healthy and unhealthy neuroception.

Healthy Neuroception: This is when your internal state accurately matches your external environment. You feel safe and connected around safe people, and your defenses (flight/fight) activate when there's a real threat.

Unhealthy Neuroception: This is a mismatch. It's when you don't feel safe even in a safe place, or you miss the red flags and don't activate your defenses in a dangerous situation.

The Real-World Impact: This concept is key to understanding why we might repeat certain patterns in relationships or why defensive states can become our default, a common thread in many mental health challenges
2422107:
The stories you tell yourself are a direct reflection of your current state. This lesson unpacks Deb Dana's concept of "Story Follows State."

Your State is Your Filter: Your autonomic state is the lens through which you see the world. This filter directly shapes your thoughts, memories, and even how you solve problems.

Different States, Different Stories: The exact same situation will generate a different internal narrative depending on where you are on your Polyvagal Ladder. A story from shutdown might sound like, "There's no point," while a story from safety sounds like, "I can do better next time."

The Self-Reinforcing Loop: These stories don't just explain your state; they can also reinforce it. A negative thought can lock you into a defensive state, creating a loop that can be hard to break
2426656:
Now it's your turn to experience "Story Follows State" in real-time. This is a hands-on experiment to notice the link between your feelings and your thoughts.

Your Task: As you view each image, pay attention to two things: the immediate story that comes to mind, and the physical or emotional feelings that arise in your body.

Feelings First, Story Second: This is a direct experience of how your feelings often come first, and your mind instantly creates a narrative to make sense of them.

No Right or Wrong Answers: Your story will be unique to you. The goal is simply to notice the automatic link between what you feel and the story you tell yourself.
2452693:
You’re very early in the unstucking process, so if this is too much for you, feel free to return to it another time.

Optional:

  • Is it possible you’ve experienced autonomic shifts that were out of your control? (A simple “yes” or “no” is sufficient for now.)

  • Is it possible that you did not choose your behavioral responses to these situations, and instead, you responded due to your Polyvagal state shift? (A simple “yes” or “no” is sufficient for now.)

  • If it’s true that your body shifted to a defensive state, how does that impact your view of this situation(s)? How does that impact your view of yourself in that moment? How about your view of yourself now?
2422097:
Welcome to the top of your Polyvagal Ladder. The Safety State is the biological foundation for health, growth, restoration, and connection.

It's Biology, Not Just an Idea: Safety is more than the absence of danger. It's a specific biological circuit (the ventral vagal) that enables social engagement and a lot more.

Automatic Social Engagement: When you're in this state, connection becomes effortless. You'll naturally smile, make eye contact, and get closer to others. Internally, you experience feelings of calm, joy, and motivation.

Perception is Everything: Your perception of danger can override your physical reality. Even in a perfectly safe environment (like watching a football game), a perceived threat can instantly knock you down the ladder into a defensive state.

Building Your Capacity for Safety: For those unfamiliar with this feeling, safety can paradoxically feel vulnerable or uncomfortable at first. It’s a state you may need to build your capacity to tolerate and enjoy over time.
2426784:
Climbing to the top of your ladder requires the right ingredients. This lesson breaks down the essential components you need to actively cultivate and access your safety state.

Safe People & Safe Environments: The two most critical components. Accessing your safety state is much easier when you have both, and ongoing, consistent opportunities to be with safe people in safe places.

Reliable, Reciprocal Relationships: It's about the quality of the connection. Safety is nurtured in relationships built on empathy, understanding, and a mutual give-and-take.

Shared Activities (Play & Work): Safety isn't passive. It's actively built by doing things together with safe people, whether it's through play or collaborative work.
2452694:
Use the questions below to reflect or journal. Don’t worry about answering all of them; use them more as inspiration.

  • Can you identify one moment in the past week when you were in your safety state? How could you tell?

  • When was the last time you made eye contact with a pet or person and were okay with it? Who were you with? What felt okay about it?

  • When did you last smile? What was happening?

  • What passive safety cues are in your life? (Think of people and places.)

  • What can you actively do to feel safe?

  • How often do you feel safe in a week?

  • What is one obstacle to safety that you can change? Is there something you can change in your environment? Is there an activity you can set up for yourself? Is there a sensory cue you can set up?
2422098:
Time to move down the ladder into the state of mobilization and defense. This is the Flight/Fight state, powered by your sympathetic nervous system.

The Goal: Create Distance: When this state is active, your primary biological goal is to create space from a perceived threat. You've moved out of connection and into protection, and you may now see others as dangerous.

Your Senses on High Alert: Your body changes to support survival. Your hearing tunes out human voices to listen for high or low-pitched danger sounds. You lose the ability to read social cues from faces, and even a neutral expression can be neurocepted as a threat.

Two Flavors of Mobilization: Flight and Fight are two sides of the same coin. Flight is about getting away from danger and is felt as anxiety, worry, or dread. If you can't get away, Fight takes over, which is about getting the danger to back off and is felt as anger and irritation.

Stuck in Survival Mode: This state is designed for short, intense bursts of energy, not long-term living. When this energy gets stuck, it can lead to chronic anxiety (stuck flight) or persistent anger and aggression (stuck fight).
2452696:
Use the questions below to reflect or journal. Don’t worry about answering all of them; use them more as inspiration.

  • Name one instance from this past week when you felt your flight/fight state active (make this something light, not serious). How could you tell?

  • When was the last time you felt irritated? Do you think you were in fight?

  • When was the last time you felt anxious? Do you think you were in flight

  • What is the easiest way you can tell you have flight activation? How about fight?

  • How difficult is it to contain your flight/fight activation?
2422099:
Now we arrive at the bottom of the ladder: the Shutdown state. This is the state of immobilization, activated when your system perceives a life threat and escape is not an option.

Biology of Immobilization: When you can't fight or flee, your body's oldest defense system takes over. This is a state of collapse, where everything slows down to conserve resources, heart rate, breathing, and blood flow. It's the biological equivalent of "playing dead."

The World Goes Gray: From inside a shutdown state, the world feels overwhelming, pointless, and disconnected. Common feelings include numbness, hopelessness, fogginess, and a profound sense of being alone or hollow.

The Gentle Climb Up: Coming out of shutdown isn't about a big burst of energy. It requires a gentle, gradual return. This is fostered by reorienting to your environment through small actions, seeking calm and quiet, and being in the presence of safe people in safe places.
2452697:
Use the questions below to reflect or journal. Don’t worry about answering all of them; use them more as inspiration.

  • Name one instance from this past week when you felt your shutdown state active. (Keep this very light and easy; nothing triggering.) How do you know it was shutdown?

  • When was the last time you felt sad?

  • When was the last time you felt like giving up?

  • When was the last time you felt numb?

  • What is the most obvious way to identify you’re in shutdown?
2422100:
What happens when your body hits the gas and the brakes at the same time? That’s the Freeze state, a complex and often misunderstood mixed state.

Not Shutdown, But a Mix: Unlike the limp collapse of shutdown, Freeze is a tense, charged combination. It's the high energy of Flight/Fight mixed with the immobilization of Shutdown.

Mobilize + Immobilize: This is the core conflict of Freeze. Your body has the powerful impulse to run away or fight, but it's simultaneously held in place, either by force or by the perception that you can't escape.

The Feeling of Panic & Overwhelm: In your daily life, this state often manifests as panic or a feeling of being completely overwhelmed. Your heart races and your muscles are tight (Flight/Fight), but you feel stuck and unable to act (Shutdown).

"Taut as a Wire" Tension: A perfect description of this state is feeling "as taut as a wire." It’s an internal battle between the desperate need to escape and the reality of being unable to move, creating immense internal pressure.
2452698:
Use the questions below to reflect or journal. Don’t worry about answering all of them; use them more as inspiration.

  • When was the last time you felt tense, overwhelmed, apprehensive, or stressed? Do you think those were mild or moderate freeze activations? How could you tell?

  • Have you tried therapies or other interventions that reinforced the freeze? How could you tell?
2422101:
Play is our next mixed state.

The Recipe for Fun: Play is the beautiful blend of your Safe & Social state with the energy of Flight/Fight. It's the biology of being mobilized and active while feeling completely safe and connected with another person.

It's a Shared Dance: True play is a reciprocal, back-and-forth experience. It relies on both people constantly sending and receiving safety cues, like smiles and eye contact, to keep the high energy from tipping into actual defense.

Your Nervous System's Gym: Play is crucial for building resilience. It's a safe way to practice moving up and down your Polyvagal Ladder, strengthening your capacity for self-regulation and your connection with others.

When Play Feels Unsafe: For some, the high energy of play can feel threatening. This happens when it's difficult to neurocept safety cues from others while mobilized, causing the body to default to a defensive state instead of a playful one.
2452700:
Use the questions below to reflect or journal. Don’t worry about answering all of them; use them more as inspiration.

  • Name one instance from this past week when you felt your play mixed state active. How do you know it was play?

  • When was the last time you felt a sense of fun? Imagination? Connection with mobility?

  • Do you have easily accessible ways of playing?

  • Do you have easily accessible people to play with?

  • When you think of playing, do any emotional obstacles occur within you? How about thoughts?

  • When was the last time you felt motivated and focused on completing a goal? How easy is it for you to feel motivated and focused on a solo task?
2422102:
The final mixed state is a quiet but powerful one: Stillness. This is the state that allows you to be calm, reflective, and at ease in your own body.

The Calm of Safe Immobilization: Stillness is the combination of your Safe & Social state with the immobilization of Shutdown. It’s the ability to be still and feel completely okay with it, without any sense of fear.

Essential for Daily Life: You use this state all the time without realizing it. It's necessary for self-reflection, meditation, intimacy, using the restroom, and getting a good night's sleep. For a child in a classroom, it's what allows them to sit calmly and learn.

When Stillness Feels Unsafe: For someone stuck in a defensive state, immobilization can trigger a neuroception of danger. Their body interprets immobility as vulnerability. This can lead to anxiety when trying to sleep, difficulty meditating, or a child struggling to sit still in class.
2452699:
Use the questions below to reflect or journal. Don’t worry about answering all of them; use them more as inspiration.

  • Name one instance from this past week when you felt your stillness mixed state active. How do you know it was stillness?

  • When was the last time you felt calm, relaxed, okay with being immobile, and connected to the present moment through your senses?

  • Can you identify any ways you cope with immobility?
2422108:
This lesson reframes the common understanding of trauma, moving from the event itself to the body's internal response.

Trauma is a Response, Not an Event: Trauma isn't what happened to you; it's the result of what happened to you - being stuck in a defensive state (flight, fight, shutdown, or freeze) on the Polyvagal ladder. Two people can experience the same scary event, but only one might become traumatized.

Sources of Trauma: The events that lead to this stuck state can come from different sources, including one-time incidents (like an accident), ongoing relentless stress (like childhood neglect), and commonly overlooked causes (like surgery or a significant breakup).

Context is Everything: A commonly overlooked event can be the final "tipping point" for a system already teetering on the edge of a defensive state.
2441647:
This first path to trauma is shaped by a single, overwhelming event. It's not about the duration, but the intensity of the moment.

An Acute Life Threat Reaction: This path results from a one-time event like a car crash, an assault, or a natural disaster. The key element is that your nervous system perceives an immediate threat to your survival.

The Biological Trap: Incomplete Survival: During the event, your body has a massive impulse to run or fight, but for some reason, you're immobilized. This can be due to physical force or the perception that escape is impossible. This traps the intense flight/fight energy in your system, leading to a stuck Freeze state.

How Triggers are Formed: Your brainstem links sensory details from the event, a specific sound, a smell, a sight, to that trapped defensive energy. Later, encountering one of those sensory triggers can feel like you're reliving the event, as it reactivates the stuck survival response.

Living with the Aftermath: People on this path can often build a fulfilling life, but they may find themselves actively avoiding anything that reminds them of the event. This avoidance of triggers becomes a way to manage the potential for being thrown back into that intense defensive state.
2422109:
This second path to trauma is not about a single moment, but about the slow, steady erosion of safety and connection over time.

A Chronic Disruption of Connection: This path is forged through repeated events that sever the impulse to connect, such as ongoing neglect, abuse, or domestic violence. It's the experience of connection being consistently unsafe or unavailable.

A Constant State of Defense: This doesn't just create a temporary reaction; it forces the autonomic nervous system to live in a chronic state of defense. Flight/Fight or Shutdown becomes the body's default setting for navigating the world.

The Impact on Childhood Attachment: Children are especially vulnerable to this path because they have a biological necessity to attach to caregivers for survival. When that need is repeatedly unmet, it disrupts the very foundation of how they learn to be in relationships and feel safe.

Challenges in Adult Relationships: Without an early blueprint for safe connection, individuals often struggle to identify or maintain healthy relationships later in life. A safe, predictable partner may feel unfamiliar or uncomfortable, as the nervous system has adapted to a world of defense.
2441777:
While the goal is to live in your Safe & Social state, it's not realistic to expect to be there all the time. The more practical aim is to have consistent access to it.

Your "Home Away From Home": This is the concept for the defensive state you exist in most often, more than your Safe & Social state. It's the state that may feel the most familiar, predictable, or even comfortable because your system has adapted to it over time.
2452701:
Use the questions below to reflect or journal. Don’t worry about answering all of them; use them more as inspiration.

And please don’t attempt to reflect on anything that is too much for you right now.

  • Can you identify events or contexts in your life that were more likely to result in path 1? (Keep it very light. Yes or No will suffice.)

  • Can you identify events or contexts in your life that were more likely to result in path 2? (Keep it very light. Yes or No will suffice.)

  • What do you think your “home away from home” is?

  • Is it possible that your stuck state is simply a result of your life's context? And not a reflection of who you are or your worth?

  • Is more connection and fulfillment possible if you emerge from your stuck defensive state?

  • What does an unstuck life look like for you? What would change in your emotions? The way you view yourself? What would family, friendships, and professional life look like?
